findings.text: follow-on: the same absent-vs-empty distinction the commit fixed for the raw tier is not applied one tier down. _raw_has_no_row returns False for any non-raw tier (line 1048: info[1] != _RAW_TIER), so a minute or hour file that is blank or holds no parseable row is still offered and can be selected by one_tier_per_job, which chooses by file presence, not by whether the file yields a job's rows. A job whose raw file is retired and whose minute compaction wrote nothing would then be pinned to an empty minute tier and its window read as uncovered while a populated hour tier sat beside it -- the identical hazard rule 1 of the retention block exists to prevent, one resolution coarser. Recorded as a residual of the node's goal rather than a defect the commit introduced: the node's brief and plan reading 10 name the raw tier only, and no in-repo path produces a blank minute beside a populated hour today (a compaction that writes nothing is exactly the case the _raw_has_no_row docstring names for the raw tier). If the tier selection is ever widened, the predicate belongs on every tier the selection ranks, not on the raw tier alone.

follow_ons.text: _holds_a_record_line now parses lines rather than testing them for non-blankness, and it is invoked from _raw_has_no_row inside ingest's per-pass offering filter (line 919) for every discovered raw file on every pass. A raw file whose every line fails to parse now costs a full lex of the file per pass until it settles, where a blank test stopped at the first byte. The common case is unchanged and cheap -- the scan stops at the first line that parses -- and the cost is bounded by the raw file, which is small against the ingest already reading it, so this is recorded rather than raised. It becomes material only for a pathologically large raw file that is unparseable end to end.
